findings.title: Team admin/owner permission check uses && instead of ||
findings.body: isTeamAdminOrOwner is computed as `(await isTeamAdmin(user.id, teamId)) && (await isTeamOwner(user.id, teamId))`. isTeamOwner is only true for users with the OWNER membership role, so any team admin who is not also the team owner fails this check and gets a FORBIDDEN ('you_do_not_have_permission') error when calling viewer.bookings.addGuests. The variable name, and the fact that the bookings UI exposes the 'Additional guests' action to team admins, indicate the intent was OR. Consequence: team admins can open the Add Guests dialog but every submission fails.

findings.title: Calendar update uses the requester's credentials instead of the booking organizer's
findings.body: The handler builds EventManager from `ctx.user` and `getUsersCredentials(ctx.user)` — the person clicking 'add guests' — but the booking's calendar reference and destination calendar belong to `booking.user` (the organizer, whose credentials were even fetched in the booking query at lines 35-40 but go unused). When anyone other than the organizer adds guests (an attendee, or a team admin/owner managing someone else's team booking), `eventManager.updateCalendarAttendees(evt, booking)` cannot find the calendar credential that owns the event, so it throws or silently skips the update. Because the attendee rows were already committed at line 92, the guests end up saved in the DB while the calendar event is never updated and the mutation returns an error; retrying then fails with 'emails_must_be_unique_valid' because the guests already exist.

findings.title: Attendees are persisted before calendar/email side effects with no transaction or idempotency
findings.body: `prisma.booking.update({ ..., attendees: { createMany } })` commits the new attendees first; only afterwards are the calendar event updated (line 165) and emails sent (line 168). If anything after the DB write fails (calendar API error, missing credential, process crash), the API returns an error even though the guests were added, and because the uniqueness filter at line 76 then treats them as existing attendees, the user cannot simply retry — the guests remain on the booking without calendar entries or invitation emails. The operation should be idempotent or the side effects performed in a way that can be recovered.

findings.title: Guest email matching is case-sensitive, bypassing the blacklist and duplicate checks
findings.body: BLACKLISTED_GUEST_EMAILS entries are lowercased (line 71) but the incoming guest is compared un-normalized (`!blacklistedGuestEmails.includes(guest)`), so 'Blocked@Example.com' bypasses a blacklist entry 'blocked@example.com'. The existing-attendee dedupe (`guest === attendee.email`) and the `newGuests.includes(attendee.email)` check in sendAddGuestsEmails have the same problem, so a case-variant of an existing attendee's email creates a duplicate Attendee row, and isAttendee (line 52) can fail to recognize an attendee whose stored email case differs from their account email. Emails should be normalized (e.g. lowercased) before all comparisons. Additionally, the input array itself is never de-duplicated server-side — the uniqueness check exists only in the client dialog's zod schema — so a direct API call containing duplicate entries creates duplicate attendees.

findings.title: Any attendee can add an unbounded number of guests to a booking
findings.body: The permission check allows anyone whose email appears on the booking — including guests who were themselves added through this feature — to add further guests, and ZAddGuestsInputSchema places no upper bound on the guests array. A single request can therefore create hundreds of Attendee rows and trigger an email to every one of them through Cal.com's mail infrastructure (a spam/abuse vector), and it discloses the meeting location/video link to arbitrary addresses without the organizer's involvement. Consider capping the number of guests per request/booking and reconsidering whether attendees (rather than only the organizer/team admins) should have this ability.

findings.title: No validation of booking status or time before adding guests
findings.body: After loading the booking the handler checks only permissions; it never verifies that the booking is still active. Guests can be added to CANCELLED or REJECTED bookings, and to bookings whose endTime is in the past (the UI even offers the action on past confirmed bookings via the Edit menu in BookingListItem). In those cases the handler inserts attendees and sends emails plus an ics with status CONFIRMED and method REQUEST for an event that is cancelled or already over, leaving attendees and calendars in a misleading state. The handler should reject cancelled/rejected (and probably past) bookings.

findings.title: Adding guests to seated bookings bypasses seat tracking
findings.body: For event types with seatsPerTimeSlot, attendees are supposed to be backed by BookingSeat reference rows; this handler inserts plain Attendee records via createMany without creating seat references and without checking remaining seat capacity. The occupied-seat count for the slot is therefore not incremented, so the slot can be overbooked beyond seatsPerTimeSlot, and the new attendee cannot be managed through seated-booking flows (e.g. cancelling an individual seat via seatReferenceUid). Either create the seat references and enforce capacity, or reject add-guests for seated event types.

findings.title: Raw guest input passed to sendAddGuestsEmails instead of the filtered uniqueGuests
findings.body: sendAddGuestsEmails decides which template each attendee receives via `newGuests.includes(attendee.email)`, but the handler passes the original `guests` array rather than `uniqueGuests`. If the request includes an address that already belongs to an existing attendee (which uniqueGuests deliberately filtered out, e.g. the organizer re-submitting an existing guest), that existing attendee is treated as 'new' and receives a full booking-confirmation email (AttendeeScheduledEmail) instead of the 'new guests added' notification.

findings.title: Team members are never notified because evt.team is never populated
findings.body: sendAddGuestsEmails contains a loop over `calendarEvent.team?.members` to send each team member an OrganizerAddGuestsEmail, but the CalendarEvent constructed in this handler has no `team` property, so that loop is dead code and team members of collective/round-robin events never receive the guests-added notification.

findings.title: Add-guests emails ignore the event type's disableStandardEmails settings
findings.body: Every neighboring sender in this file (sendLocationChangeEmails, sendRescheduledEmails, sendCancelledEmails, etc.) accepts eventTypeMetadata and skips host/attendee emails via eventTypeDisableHostEmail/eventTypeDisableAttendeeEmail. sendAddGuestsEmails takes no metadata and the calling handler never reads eventType.metadata, so organizers who disabled standard emails for an event type still have 'guests added' emails sent to themselves, their team, and all attendees — violating a user-facing event-type setting.

findings.title: Untranslated 'Remove email' tooltip string
findings.body: The remove-button tooltip uses the hardcoded English string "Remove email" instead of t(...) with a key in the locale files (the component otherwise uses useLocale), so it renders in English for every locale and is not pickable by the translation tooling.

findings.title: No tests for the new addGuests mutation
findings.body: The PR introduces a new authenticated mutation with non-trivial authorization logic (organizer vs team admin/owner vs attendee), dedupe/blacklist filtering, calendar updates, and email fan-out, but adds no tests. Handler tests over the permission matrix and error paths would have caught regressions such as the && / || mix-up in isTeamAdminOrOwner and the wrong-credential EventManager construction.
